name: Mikado Brown
lede: Mikado Brown is a light, tan-leaning brown from Ridgway's 1912 color atlas, named for the Japanese imperial title rather than for any dye or wood.

sections.title: A title, used as a color word
sections.body:
Ridgway's atlas places this value at plate XXIX, hue 13′′, tone i, first recorded in 1912 [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary lands on the same year at plate 14, position C 9, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 classifies the hue as a moderate brown [1][2]. *Mikado* was, at the time, a common English word for the Emperor of Japan; Ridgway gives no further reason for attaching it to this particular tan-brown rather than any other [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[french-beige]], [[brown-sugar]] and [[india-spice]], at 3, 3.4 and 3.5 ΔE [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Mikado Brown covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 1,337 works, about one in eighteen, as photographed [3]. Its earliest match is an ancient Egyptian funerary papyrus; it peaks in the 1270s, in 13 of 48 paintings, and is strongest in Tibet, India and Iran, with Hans Memling, Albrecht Dürer and Lucas Cranach among the painters who carry it far above their average, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. That breadth across so many centuries and places likely reflects how common a light tan-brown is in aged parchment and varnish generally, not one pigment [3]. These remain photographs of aged, varnished works read as screen colors [3].
